subject: ela
intro: Each item gives you a short paragraph or a claim with a brief source. Read carefully and weigh the options, because more than one choice may look reasonable. Choose the part that best fits the argument and explain your thinking using the answer key.

items.prompt: Claim: 'Our school should start a recycling program.' Reason: 'A recycling program would cut down the amount of trash the school sends to the landfill.' Read the source: 'A 2022 district audit found that the school throws away about 400 pounds of paper and plastic each week, almost all of which could be recycled.' Which detail is the most relevant evidence for this reason: (1) the 400 pounds of recyclable waste each week, (2) the school colors are blue and white, or (3) recycling bins come in many sizes? Write the number and explain why it best supports the reason.
items.answer: (1) the 400 pounds of recyclable waste each week.

steps: The reason claims a recycling program would reduce landfill trash, so the evidence must show how much recyclable waste currently goes to the landfill.
Detail (1) gives a specific, credible statistic from the audit showing 400 pounds of recyclable material is thrown away weekly, which directly supports the reason.
Detail (2), the school colors, is true but off topic and does nothing to support the claim.
Detail (3), bin sizes, is about the topic of recycling but does not show a need to reduce landfill waste, so it is not relevant evidence for this reason.

items.prompt: Read this short paragraph from a student argument: 'Students should have more time to eat lunch. Right now lunch is only twenty minutes long, and many students cannot finish their food. The cafeteria also serves tacos on Tuesdays. A longer lunch would let students eat a full meal and feel ready to learn.' One sentence does not support the claim and should be removed. Write the sentence that should be cut and explain why.
items.answer: The sentence 'The cafeteria also serves tacos on Tuesdays.' should be removed.

steps: The claim is that students should have more time to eat lunch.
The sentences about the twenty-minute lunch and feeling ready to learn give reasons and evidence that support that claim.
The taco sentence is true and is about the cafeteria, but it does nothing to show that students need more time to eat.
Because it does not support the claim, it is irrelevant and should be cut from the argument.

items.prompt: Read the two sentences: 'Students who get enough sleep concentrate better in class. ______ they tend to remember more of what they study.' Which transition best fills the blank to clarify the relationship: 'However,' 'In contrast,' 'In addition,' or 'Although'? Write your choice and explain why it fits.

steps: The second sentence adds another benefit of getting enough sleep, so it builds on the first sentence rather than opposing it.
'In addition' signals that another supporting point is being added, which matches the relationship.
'However' and 'In contrast' signal a contrast or disagreement, but the two sentences agree, so they are wrong.
'Although' sets up a contrast or concession and would make the sentence incomplete, so it does not fit.

items.prompt: Read this sentence from a student argument: 'Honestly, banning gum at school is super dumb and totally unfair, so they should just stop it.' Rewrite the sentence so it keeps a formal style appropriate for an argument while making the same point. Then explain what you changed.
items.answer: A formal revision such as: 'The school's gum ban is unreasonable and should be reconsidered.'

steps: The original uses informal fillers ('Honestly'), slang ('super dumb,' 'totally'), and a vague pronoun ('they'), none of which fit a formal argument.
A formal revision removes the slang and filler and replaces emotional words with measured language, for example: 'The school's gum ban is unreasonable and should be reconsidered.'
The revision keeps the writer's position, that the gum ban should be changed, while sounding objective and credible.
Maintaining a formal style makes an argument more convincing to a reader.

items.prompt: Claim: 'The town should add a bike lane on Main Street.' Reason: 'A bike lane would make riding to school safer.' Read the source: 'A city traffic report recorded 11 bicycle accidents on Main Street last year, most caused by cars passing too closely.' Which choice is the strongest evidence for the reason: (1) 'because biking is a good idea,' (2) the report of 11 accidents from cars passing too closely, or (3) 'many people in town own bikes'? Write the number and explain why.
items.answer: (2) the report of 11 accidents from cars passing too closely.

steps: The reason is that a bike lane would make riding safer, so the evidence must show that riding is currently unsafe.
Choice (2) is a concrete statistic from a credible city report showing 11 accidents caused by cars passing too closely, which directly supports the need for a safer bike lane.
Choice (1) is just an opinion restatement, not evidence, because it gives no fact or example.
Choice (3), that many people own bikes, is related to the topic but does not show that riding is unsafe, so it does not support this reason.

items.prompt: Read the two sentences: 'The library has very few new books for students to borrow. ______ the school should set aside money to update the collection.' Which transition best fills the blank: 'For example,' 'Therefore,' 'However,' or 'In contrast'? Write your choice and explain the logical relationship.

steps: The first sentence states a problem, and the second sentence states what should be done because of that problem.
This is a cause-and-effect relationship, so a word that signals a conclusion or result is needed.
'Therefore' signals that the second sentence follows as a result of the first, which fits.
'For example' would introduce an example, and 'However' and 'In contrast' signal contrast, none of which match a cause-and-result relationship.

items.prompt: Read this paragraph from a student argument: 'Field trips help students learn in new ways. They let students see real places connected to their lessons. Field trips also give students a break from sitting in class. My cousin went to a water park last summer. These experiences make learning more memorable.' One sentence is irrelevant to the argument. Write the sentence that should be removed and explain why.
items.answer: The sentence 'My cousin went to a water park last summer.' should be removed.

steps: The claim is that field trips help students learn in new ways.
The sentences about seeing real places, getting a break, and making learning memorable all support that claim.
The cousin's water park trip is a personal detail that is not a school field trip and does not support the claim about learning.
Because it does not connect to the argument, it should be cut.

items.prompt: Claim: 'Sixth graders should be allowed to choose their own seats.' Read these two possible reasons. Reason A: 'Choosing seats lets students sit near friends.' Reason B: 'Students who choose their seats take more responsibility for their behavior and focus.' Which reason gives stronger support for an argument, and why? Write the letter and explain.
items.answer: Reason B, because it connects seat choice to responsibility and focus, which are reasons a school would value.

steps: A strong reason in an argument supports the claim in a way that a reader, such as a teacher or principal, would find convincing.
Reason B links choosing seats to better responsibility and focus, which are goals the school cares about, so it builds a logical case.
Reason A, sitting near friends, mostly serves the students' wishes and could even raise a concern about being distracted, so it is weaker support.
Therefore Reason B is the stronger reason for the argument.

items.prompt: Read this sentence from a student argument: 'Everybody already knows that long homework is a total nightmare and it stinks, so teachers need to chill out and cut it back.' Rewrite the sentence to maintain a formal style while keeping the same position. Then explain your changes.
items.answer: A formal revision such as: 'Lengthy homework assignments place a heavy burden on students, so teachers should consider reducing them.'

steps: The original uses slang ('total nightmare,' 'it stinks,' 'chill out') and an overgeneralization ('Everybody already knows'), which are not appropriate in a formal argument.

A formal revision removes the slang and sweeping claim and uses measured, objective language, for example: 'Lengthy homework assignments place a heavy burden on students, so teachers should consider reducing them.'
The revision keeps the writer's position that homework should be reduced.
Formal language makes the argument sound more credible and persuasive.

items.prompt: Claim: 'The school should offer an after-school coding club.' Reason: 'Many students want to learn computer skills that could help them in future jobs.' Read the source: 'In a recent survey, 72 percent of sixth graders said they would join a club to learn coding, and a labor report lists computer skills among the most in-demand job skills.' Which choice is the most relevant evidence for the reason: (1) the survey result and labor report, (2) 'coding clubs are fun,' or (3) the school building has a computer lab? Write the number and explain.
items.answer: (1) the survey result and labor report.

steps: The reason is that students want computer skills that could help in future jobs, so the evidence must show both the student interest and the job value.
Choice (1) provides a survey statistic showing strong student interest and a labor report showing the job value, so it directly supports the reason.
Choice (2), that clubs are fun, is an opinion, not evidence, and does not address future jobs.
Choice (3), that there is a computer lab, is about the topic but does not show student interest or job demand, so it is weaker support.

items.prompt: Read the two sentences: 'Recess gives students a chance to exercise and burn off energy. ______ some teachers worry that recess takes time away from lessons.' Which transition best fills the blank: 'In addition,' 'Therefore,' 'For instance,' or 'However'? Write your choice and explain the relationship.

steps: The first sentence states a benefit of recess, and the second sentence presents a concern that opposes it.
This is a contrast, so a transition that signals opposition is needed.
'However' signals contrast, which fits the shift from a benefit to a worry.
'In addition' and 'For instance' add or illustrate, and 'Therefore' shows a result, none of which match the contrasting relationship.

items.prompt: Read this paragraph from a student argument: 'The school should plant trees on the front lawn. Trees provide shade so students can stay cool during outdoor lunch. Trees also help clean the air around the building. The principal drives a blue car to work. For these reasons, planting trees would improve the school.' One sentence is irrelevant. Write the sentence that should be removed and explain why.
items.answer: The sentence 'The principal drives a blue car to work.' should be removed.

steps: The claim is that the school should plant trees on the front lawn.
The sentences about shade and cleaner air give reasons that support the claim.
The detail about the principal's blue car is unrelated to trees or to improving the school, so it does not support the argument.
Because it is off topic, it should be removed.

items.prompt: Read this short argument: 'The school should add water bottle filling stations. Students often run out of water during the day, and the only fountains are slow and crowded. Filling stations would help everyone stay hydrated and healthy.' Which sentence would be the best concluding statement: (1) 'In conclusion, water bottle filling stations would keep students hydrated and ease the crowding at the fountains.', (2) 'In conclusion, the cafeteria should also serve more salads.', or (3) 'In conclusion, the fountains are slow.'? Write the number and explain.
items.answer: (1) 'In conclusion, water bottle filling stations would keep students hydrated and ease the crowding at the fountains.'

steps: A good concluding statement restates the claim and reflects the reasons given in the argument.
Choice (1) restates the call for filling stations and reflects both reasons, hydration and crowded fountains, so it follows from the whole argument.
Choice (2) introduces a brand-new idea about salads that the argument never discussed, so it does not follow.
Choice (3) only repeats one minor detail and does not restate the claim, so it is too narrow to serve as a conclusion.

items.prompt: Claim: 'The school should keep the art program.' Read these two possible evidence choices for the reason 'Art helps students do better in other subjects.' Evidence A: 'A 2021 study found that students enrolled in art classes scored higher on reading and math tests than students who were not.' Evidence B: 'Art class is the favorite class of many students.' Which choice is the stronger, more relevant evidence, and why? Write the letter and explain.
items.answer: Evidence A, because it gives a credible study linking art to higher scores in other subjects.

steps: The reason is that art helps students do better in other subjects, so the evidence must connect art to performance in those subjects.
Evidence A reports a study showing art students scored higher in reading and math, which directly supports that reason with a credible fact.
Evidence B says art is a favorite class, which shows students enjoy it but does not show it improves performance in other subjects.
Therefore Evidence A is the stronger, more relevant evidence.

items.prompt: Read this sentence from a student argument: 'I think we should totally get rid of the dress code because it's annoying and my friends all hate it too.' Rewrite the sentence to maintain a formal style and rely on a reasoned point rather than personal feelings. Then explain your changes.
items.answer: A formal revision such as: 'The dress code should be revised because it limits students' ability to express themselves comfortably.'

steps: The original uses first-person filler ('I think'), slang ('totally'), and personal feelings ('it's annoying,' 'my friends all hate it') instead of a reasoned point.
A formal revision states a position and gives a reasoned basis, for example: 'The dress code should be revised because it limits students' ability to express themselves comfortably.'
The revision keeps the writer's position that the dress code should change while removing slang and emotional appeals.
Relying on a reason rather than feelings makes the argument more convincing and appropriate for a formal style.
